title: Service Decomposition

sections.title: Tenant Isolation at the Data Boundary

html:
Baodium began as one Rails application maintained by five engineers. Catalog, Checkout, and Inventory code ran in the same process against the same database, so a feature that needed product data could join another team’s table, and related updates could commit in one transaction. For a team of five, that was fast and sensible, and most systems start the same way. By the time the company had forty engineers, Catalog and Order Service, which implemented checkout, had separate repositories and deployment pipelines. Order Service, however, still read Catalog’s products table directly when it checked whether cart items were eligible for sale.

During a merchandising update, the Catalog team added a nullable column called display_weight and populated it from existing rows. The migration passed staging. In production, however, the migration tool ran both the table alteration and the lengthy backfill in one transaction. The alteration acquired an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and PostgreSQL released it only when the transaction committed. Order Service’s eligibility reads queued behind it, and affected customers could not complete checkout for about thirty minutes.

Two days later, Catalog proposed another change to the same table. Checkout asked for a review of every future migration because a schema change had just interrupted orders. Catalog wanted to be able to update its own data without requiring another team’s approval. The teams had separate deployment pipelines, but the database contract between them had never been agreed upon.

In 1968, Melvin Conway observed that organizations tend to build systems that reflect their communication structure.1 The observation, now called Conway’s Law, explains why this chapter is about teams as much as code. Catalog could deploy without coordinating its schema change with Checkout, yet the two teams still shared the database table on which checkout depended.

PostgreSQL Migration Lock and Recovery

It is tempting to respond to an incident like this by redrawing the architecture. The direct cause, however, was the migration procedure, and fixing it required no new service or database. You saw the safe pattern in Chapter 10. In PostgreSQL, adding a nullable column without a default is normally a metadata-only change, but it still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Even a brief change can wait behind another transaction, so the migration uses a short lock_timeout. The mistake at Baodium was running the backfill in the same transaction. Committing the column change separately, then backfilling in small transactions while application code accepts rows with a null value, avoids that prolonged lock. The backfill still uses database CPU, row locks, and I/O, so its rate needs testing alongside ordinary traffic, just as Chapter 10 described.

Migration tools differ in their transaction defaults. Some wrap an entire migration in one transaction, so the team must check that behavior before combining schema changes with a long backfill. Separating the steps also makes each failure easier to recover from.

The responder also needed clear options during the incident. The first step is to find the session that is blocking everyone else, and PostgreSQL can show you directly with the query in Listing Listing.

Stopping the blocker takes some care. Canceling its statement with pg_cancel_backend inside a transaction opened with BEGIN leaves the transaction open, in an aborted state, and its locks are released only when the client rolls it back. Terminating the session with pg_terminate_backend ends the transaction and releases its locks, at the cost of discarding its uncommitted work. Setting idle_in_transaction_session_timeout also protects you from a related problem, in which a client opens a transaction, stops sending statements, and never releases its locks.

The migration procedure needed correction regardless of how the application was organized. The open architectural decision was who could change the product data on which Checkout depended. As long as Order Service queried Catalog’s tables directly, a future schema change could interrupt checkout without crossing an API boundary.

Release, Runtime, and Data Boundaries

When people talk about splitting a system into services, they often mean several different separations bundled together, and each one solves a different problem. Figure Figure separates three kinds of coupling inside one application, and Figure Figure shows what splitting into services removes and what it leaves behind.

Table Table lists the four separations an extraction can provide, together with the dependencies each one leaves for you to examine.

Each separation stops one kind of interference and leaves the others in place. Separate processes prevent a Catalog crash from taking down Order Service, but they do not stop Catalog’s queries from using shared database capacity. Separate schemas and database roles can enforce ownership on a single database server, which may be all the protection a team needs against unauthorized writes and undocumented table access, although both domains still share the server’s CPU, I/O, and maintenance operations. Dedicated database instances separate those resources as well, but each instance needs its own capacity planning, backups, restore tests, credentials, and operational support, so the benefit has to justify the extra responsibility.

The Modular Monolith

You do not need a network call to enforce a useful boundary. Inside a single application, a Catalog module can own product data and expose operations to other modules, and Checkout can use those operations without importing Catalog’s persistence code or writing its own product queries. This arrangement is often called a modular monolith. It retains local calls and transactions while making unauthorized dependencies easy to spot.

The enforcement can be automated. In a Rails application like Baodium’s original one, Shopify’s Packwerk checks that one package references another only through its declared public interface. Java teams use ArchUnit for the same purpose, and Python teams use import-linter. A violation then fails the build, the same way a broken test does.

A modular monolith is also the cheapest place to find out whether a boundary is in the right position. Inside one codebase, a violation is a failed build and redrawing the boundary is one refactoring commit. Across a network, the same mistake becomes a production incident and a migration project. For a system whose responsibilities are still being worked out, this is often the better choice. Extracting a service becomes more attractive when a specific requirement calls for independent deployment, a separate resource allocation, restricted access, or a distinct operating owner. At Baodium, Catalog already had its own team and release process, so the open work concerned its consumers and who could change its authoritative records.

Domain Ownership and Bounded Contexts

A database table is an implementation detail, so assigning tables to services is the wrong place to start. Start instead with the decisions the records support. For each kind of record, ask who makes the decision it supports, what information that decision needs, and how current that information has to be. Those three facts usually draw the line between services more accurately than the schema does. At Baodium, the product-related information served the purposes in Table Table.

The word product refers to two records with different lifetimes. Catalog owns a listing that merchants can edit, reprice, and retire. Checkout needs the product details the customer accepted when placing the order, even if the listing changes later. Editing a product title should not rewrite the description on an existing order, so Checkout records the relevant description and the accepted terms when the order is created, and Catalog goes on maintaining the current listing. It also lets customers view past purchases during a Catalog outage.

You will find the same distinction far outside online shopping. An airline stores the fare a passenger accepted at booking, even after the fare table changes. An invoice records the price in effect when it was issued. A signed contract preserves the terms as signed, while the template it came from is revised. In each case, one record describes something that can change, and another records what was agreed at a particular moment.

Domain-driven design calls the area within which a term has one agreed meaning a bounded context. Recognizing that Catalog and Checkout are separate contexts tells the engineers which information Checkout can copy and which operations must go through Catalog. Team responsibilities track the same lines, so Catalog’s owner is responsible for its contracts, schema, capacity, and recovery. If every internal change to Catalog needs approval from several teams, look for the dependency that is forcing that coordination, rather than accepting it as the normal cost of working together.

Transaction Boundaries

Pay particular attention wherever a single transaction currently enforces a business rule, because a split at that point can break correctness. Inventory, for example, creates a reservation and reduces the available quantity in one local transaction. Splitting those two updates across services would require a protocol for the case in which one commits and the other fails. Baodium avoided that by defining reservation as a single Inventory operation. Checkout requests a reservation, rather than reading a quantity and later sending a separate decrement, so the rule is still enforced inside one transaction owned by one service. The general rule is that any two pieces of data that must change together should have the same owner, or the business has to accept, and design for, the moments when they disagree.

Catalog’s sale-eligibility check needed similar thought. Reading that a product was sellable just before confirming an order did not stop a merchant from withdrawing the product between the read and the order commit, and replacing the read with an API call would not close that gap either. A response from the responsible service is authoritative, but it does not form an atomic transaction with the caller’s commit. The engineers and the product owner had to decide when an eligibility decision became binding. One contract could treat a decision as valid for a given operation until an expiry time, accepting that a product withdrawn in that window might still be sold. Another could require that a withdrawal block every later acceptance, including orders already in progress, which needs a reservation-like operation or placing the decision and the order commit under one owner. Settling that before the extraction mattered, because discovering a missing correctness rule after two databases already accept independent writes is far more expensive to fix.

Decision review

Extract, or fix the boundary in place?

Checkout reads Catalog’s products table directly. A Catalog migration has already halted checkout once. The team is considering four responses, and has roughly one quarter of engineering time available.

Give the existing Catalog service its own database and replace Checkout’s direct table access with the Catalog contract.

Retain one database, but revoke Checkout’s table access and put a Catalog-owned interface in front of it.

Allow direct access and require migrations to run in small, non-blocking steps.

Copy the fields Checkout needs into Checkout’s own tables.

C fixes the migration’s immediate locking problem by separating the schema change from the backfill and testing the batches, but direct table access leaves Checkout coupled to Catalog’s schema.

B replaces that direct access with a Catalog-owned contract, so Catalog can change its implementation as long as it preserves the contract. Both services can still be slowed by locks and resource contention in the shared database, even though they no longer share an application connection pool.

A separates database ownership and can reduce that contention, but it adds a network call, availability requirements for the Catalog service, and a data migration. Shared infrastructure and synchronous dependencies need their own failure handling, and an interface already in place from B makes the later extraction easier.

D gives Checkout a local copy for reads that can tolerate its update delay. A purchase decision that needs current sale eligibility still needs an authoritative check, or another contract that preserves that requirement.

Fix the migration first, then choose B, A, or D according to the independent changes and read guarantees the teams need. A quarter of engineering time is a planning constraint, not evidence that any option will fit without an implementation estimate.

Consumer Contracts

Order Service queried Catalog’s schema to decide whether each cart item could be accepted for sale, so the replacement contract had to return that decision without exposing Catalog’s internal columns. A generic endpoint that returned every product field would leave Order Service interpreting Catalog’s internal state, which recreates the original coupling over HTTP. A bounded assessment operation instead accepts the cart’s product references and returns a separate result for each item. An unknown product, an ineligible product, and an assessment that could not be completed are separate results, because a timeout is not evidence that a product does not exist.

Request cost needs attention too. Replacing one SQL query with one network request per cart line would add many calls to every order acceptance, so the operation takes the whole cart in one batch, with a maximum batch size and a defined result for items whose assessment did not complete. Authorization also has to work across the new boundary. A service identity establishes which application is calling, while tenant and user rules decide which records it may access on a customer’s behalf.

Whatever you use to describe the contract, an OpenAPI document or a Protocol Buffers definition, store it where both teams review it, and let consumer contract tests, as described in Chapter 10, catch incompatible changes before they reach production.

Conditional API Updates

An API contract also needs to define what happens when two clients update the same resource. Imagine two merchant employees editing a shipping rule. Both read revision 7. One changes the permitted destinations, while the other updates a cutoff time. If the API accepts both full-document replacements without checking the original revision, the second request can overwrite the first employee’s change.

One approach is to return an entity tag (ETag) with the resource. The client sends that version back in an If-Match header when it updates the resource.

For this example, the API treats the submitted body as the complete editable representation. The server compares the supplied revision with the current revision inside the same database transaction that applies the update. If another employee has already published revision 8, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed and the client retrieves the current policy before deciding how to merge the changes.2

The comparison must use the representation’s version and the resource owner’s authoritative store. Comparing a cached version before writing through another connection could recreate the race. This is optimistic concurrency control, and it fits collaborative configuration, document editing, and administrative APIs. It is different from an idempotency key. One controls whether a retry repeats an operation, while the other rejects a write based on an obsolete resource version.

Required Synchronous Decisions

The migration also has a less visible dependency. If Order Service requires a current Catalog assessment before accepting an order, a Catalog outage still stops new orders, even after Catalog has its own database. A migration that blocks Catalog’s assessment query now affects checkout through the API instead of through the table. Extraction removes direct schema access and lets Catalog control its own queries, admission, and responses, and Order Service can bound the call with the deadlines and concurrency limits from Chapter 4. The business dependency, however, is still there.

Any availability claim for the extraction has to reflect that. Historical orders can be displayed from stored order details, whereas new orders that need Catalog’s current decision receive the agreed unavailable or deferred response. A circuit breaker can contain resource use during a Catalog outage, but it cannot supply the missing business decision. Every system works this way. Putting a dependency behind an API changes how it fails, and the caller still needs what it provides.

Local Read Projections

The alternative to calling the owner on every request is to maintain a local copy, called a projection when one service maintains it from another service’s changes. A projection suits consumers that can tolerate delayed updates. A browsing page can show a new description a few seconds late, and a projection of stock levels can support display while actual reservations go through Inventory. Sale eligibility may need stricter treatment than descriptive text, because each consumer’s use of the information sets its freshness requirement.

A projection is like the printed timetable at a bus stop, a copy of the transit authority’s schedule. It is perfectly useful until the schedule changes, and its value depends on knowing when it was printed. Every projection likewise needs a permitted freshness interval, evidence that updates are being processed, and a defined response when that evidence is missing. The time since a product last changed is not that evidence, because a product that has not changed in months can be perfectly current. This is the idle-replica trap from Chapter 7 in another form. The consumer needs to know how far it has progressed through the source’s change history, including periods in which no relevant record changed.

Incremental Extraction

Baodium improved the contract before transferring any data, in the three stages of Figure Figure, each of which removes one kind of sharing.

Replacing one caller’s direct table access at a time is often called the strangler pattern, after the strangler fig, a vine that wraps around a tree and gradually takes over its structure. Each step is small and reversible, so a mistake affects one caller rather than the whole system. For Order Service’s eligibility query, Baodium used nine steps, each with a check that had to pass before the next one began.

  1. Local adapter. Put Order Service’s product SQL behind a CatalogClient interface inside Order Service, which still queries the shared tables. Check: no product-table SQL exists outside the adapter.

  2. Contract operations. Redesign the adapter’s operations while they are still local calls and cheap to change. One cart assessment replaced ten per-item lookups before any network round trip existed.

  3. Contract tests. Catalog publishes the assessment schema and item-level results, and Order Service’s tests run against it. Check: an incompatible Catalog change fails Catalog’s build.

  4. Remote endpoint. Catalog serves the assessment from its own process, initially reading the same shared tables.

  5. Shadow comparison. The adapter calls both implementations, returns the local result, and records any mismatch. Check: over seven days, which included the weekly price import, mismatches were below one per 100,000 assessments, and each had a known cause.

  6. Selected callers. Route 1, then 10, then 100 percent of assessments to the remote endpoint, applying the unavailable-result policy from the dependency inventory.

  7. Revoke table permission. Remove the Order Service role’s access to Catalog’s tables.

  8. Transfer data ownership. Transfer Catalog’s tables to their own database, as described in Section Section.

  9. Delete the compatibility path. Remove the local implementation and the shadow code from Order Service.

The steps run in this order for a reason. Redesigning the operations in step 2, while they are still function calls, lets the team fix a chatty interface before it costs a network round trip per item. The shadow comparison in step 5 shows that the remote endpoint returns the same results before any customer depends on it. Libraries such as GitHub’s Scientist were built for this kind of side-by-side comparison. Step 7 is the one that proves the boundary exists. Until the permission is gone, a forgotten report, script, or code path can still read the tables, and the inventory of consumers is still unverified. Listing Listing shows the revocation and the check that confirms it.

The confirming query matters more than the REVOKE itself. A role can still reach a table through a grant to PUBLIC or through membership in another role, and has_table_privilege takes both into account, which a quick look at the REVOKE statement does not.

The team revoked the permission first in staging and then in production, during business hours, with the previous grant script ready to run, and watched for permission errors from every role. A permission error from an unexpected job pointed to a dependency the inventory had missed. Because Catalog already ran as its own process, step 4 added an endpoint rather than a new service, and most of the effort went into steps 5 through 8.

Dependency Inventory

Searching the code found many readers and writers, but not all of them. The engineers also reviewed database activity, service accounts, scheduled jobs, reporting tools, imports, administrative scripts, foreign keys, and recovery procedures, and recorded a replacement and an owner for each dependency, as in Listing Listing.

Separate database roles for each application made this work possible. With one role per application, every query can be traced to its source. The pg_stat_statements extension, for instance, records statistics for each statement by the role that ran it, so a query against the inventory tables from an unexpected role stands out. With shared credentials, you cannot tell which application issued a query or what else will break when access is removed.

Runtime evidence needs an observation period that matches the workload, because a monthly report will not appear in one day of query statistics. Configuration review and conversations with owners fill the gaps that observation misses. New cross-domain writes were also prohibited during the migration, because otherwise the engineers could finish replacing one dependency while another team introduced a new one.

Data Authority Transfer

Transferring Catalog’s tables to their own database creates a period in which two databases contain the same records, and the plan has to state which one is authoritative for each record at every moment. You have seen this kind of transfer before. Chapter 7 transferred one merchant to a dedicated shard in five stages, which were copy, catch up, fence, final apply and verify, and transfer authority. Transferring a whole domain to a new database uses the same stages, and Baodium again maintained one authoritative source throughout, copying and synchronizing the destination from it, rather than writing to both databases independently and risking a failure between the two commits. What differed this time were the tools and the risks that came with them.

Snapshot and Change Capture

The transfer used PostgreSQL’s logical replication, which takes a consistent snapshot of the source tables and then streams every change committed after that snapshot. The snapshot and the starting position of the change stream have to be taken at the same moment. If you exported a table first and started change capture afterward, writes committed during the export could be lost.

Logical replication copies rows and leaves out the objects around them. Indexes, constraints, permissions, and sequence values had to be created or checked separately on the destination, and sequence values in particular had to be advanced before the destination accepted new inserts, or new records could reuse existing identifiers. Verification covered updates and deletions as well as inserts. Matching row totals can hide incorrect values, so the comparison also covered aligned key ranges and business properties such as tenant ownership, product identity, and required relationships. Each comparison used a known synchronization position on both sides, so that replication delay could not be mistaken for a conversion error.

The change stream also needed monitoring. A logical replication slot retains the source’s WAL until the destination confirms it has applied the changes, so if the destination stops applying them, the retained WAL accumulates and can fill the production database’s disk. Setting max_slot_wal_keep_size puts an upper limit on that retention, at the cost of invalidating the slot if the limit is reached, and the plan included a procedure for pausing or abandoning the transfer before that point. Throughout synchronization, the source accepted authoritative writes, and decisions that required current data used the source.

Write Cutover

For the final switch, the team chose a brief pause in product updates rather than a more elaborate live cutover, because a pause makes the final state much easier to verify and merchants could tolerate a few minutes without editing listings. Reads continued wherever their contract permitted, and the cutover took six steps.

  1. Stop admitting new writes through every legacy write path.

  2. Complete or abort active source write transactions, and prevent old processes from starting new ones.

  3. Record the final source change position after those transactions have ended.

  4. Apply destination changes through that position, and verify the required data and constraints.

  5. Enable destination writes through Catalog, and direct approved writers to it.

  6. Verify that attempts through legacy write paths are refused.

Changing credentials does not stop transactions that are already running, so the fencing in step 2 covers existing sessions, pooled connections, scheduled jobs, and privileged tools. The final position is recorded only after those writers have stopped, because a destination that reported itself caught up a moment earlier may be missing the last accepted update.

Which way you can recover depends on how far the cutover has gone. Before destination writes begin, a failed verification can return control to the source without loss. Once Catalog accepts writes at the destination, the source is an outdated copy unless verified reverse synchronization exists, and sending writes back to it would require another full transfer of authority, or accepted changes could be lost and two conflicting histories created. The team rehearsed failures at each step, so that a responder would always know which database was authoritative and which recovery action was allowed.

Legacy Retirement

Consumers lost direct table access once they had adopted the Catalog contract, and the source copy was retained under restricted access for the agreed verification and retention period, so that no application could fall back on it. Historical orders retained their accepted details and product references, and Catalog’s deletion policy took those references into account, so that retiring a listing never made a past order impossible to interpret. Reporting consumers received approved analytical copies or exports instead of operational access, because unrestricted access for reporting tools would create new schema dependencies outside the contract.

Event-Driven Projections

Once Catalog controlled its own writes, it could publish changes for search, browsing, and other consumers that accept delayed updates. Each consumer maintains a projection that stores only what it needs, in a form suited to its own queries. Search might store descriptions and categories, while another consumer stores only product identity and display attributes. Before anyone builds a projection, the team assigns responsibility for detecting differences from the source and repairing missing or outdated records, because without that responsibility, a projection drifts silently.

The mechanics are the ones from Chapter 3. Catalog commits each business update and its outbox record in one transaction, and the consumer commits each projection update together with its processing marker. Two details apply specifically to projections. If the consumer committed the marker before the update, a crash between the two would leave the event marked as processed without changing the projection, so the two must commit together. And duplicate detection does not solve ordering, because two separate events for the same product can arrive in the wrong order. Each event carries a source version, and the consumer ignores any event older than the version it has already applied.

Each consumer also needs freshness monitoring, handling for records that fail to apply, and a rebuild procedure, because a projection reduces the synchronous dependency only for the operations and the delay its contract permits. Chapter 12 examines delivery, ordering, and replay in detail. Not every relationship has to begin as a synchronous call and become asynchronous later, though. A consumer can use events from the start once ownership and its processing contract are clear.

Service Extraction Sequence

Every additional service needs deployment, capacity management, credentials, telemetry, recovery procedures, and an operating owner. Its callers take on network failures and compatibility obligations, and any copied data needs repair and reconciliation. All of that continues long after the migration project ends. An extraction creates another service owner, an on-call rotation, and a long-lived API contract. The benefits need to justify those obligations.

A service with a small codebase can still be expensive to run on its own, especially when every feature needs coordinated deployments across several services. The term distributed monolith describes this condition, in which separately running applications are still tightly coupled. The label is less useful than naming the specific mechanism. At Baodium, direct table access prevented independent schema changes. In another system, a shared library might force simultaneous upgrades, or a chain of synchronous calls might make one user action depend on the availability of many services. Some coordination reflects a genuine business requirement and is justified, while dependencies that serve no current purpose are the ones to question.

Service Extraction Priorities

Baodium selected service boundaries by the coordination they would remove and the correctness rules they would preserve. Catalog had a clear owner and many read consumers, so extracting its data authority reduced schema coupling. Inventory retained quantity changes and reservation identity in one transaction. Notifications could run after order acceptance using a durable event. A tightly interleaved pricing calculation was better served by an internal module until separate deployment offered a measurable advantage.

Choosing this way, rather than by table total or code size, means the team picks a benefit it can demonstrate and recovery work it can support. You can use these criteria for any system you are thinking of splitting.

Boundary Verification

An extraction needs tests that show the result it was meant to produce. For Catalog, the first check was that Order Service’s database role could no longer read or write product tables. The engineers then exercised the replacement contract with Catalog unavailable, delayed, and returning item-level results. Historical orders continued to display from stored details, and new orders that required a Catalog assessment took their unavailable or deferred path, with a fast rejection recorded as a failed checkout rather than a successful one.

A migration rehearsal then blocked the relevant Catalog query on purpose and confirmed the same behavior, which stopped the team from assuming that a dedicated database had removed the synchronous business dependency. Cutover tests confirmed that the destination contained the final accepted source changes, that legacy writes were refused, and that no tested failure could leave both databases accepting authoritative writes. Projection tests paused processing, checked the response to stale data, and rebuilt a copy using the approved procedure.

The engineers also checked ordinary development, because day-to-day work is where an extraction proves its value. Could Catalog change an internal table without deploying Order Service? Did contract tests catch an incompatible response? Could each team diagnose its part of a failed request without unrestricted access to the other team’s database? The results showed what the extraction had achieved, and which coordination requirements were still in place.

Policy Ownership and Service Contracts

The same way of drawing boundaries, from decisions rather than tables, works for internal tools too. Imagine your organization wants one place to publish deployment policies, validate changes, check Jira approvals, notify Slack, and record an audit history. In the first design review, someone sketches five microservices, one per feature. It seems tidy on the whiteboard, but it adds network calls and separate data stores before anyone has asked which operations need their own authority.

Start with the operations instead. Publishing a policy revision changes the authoritative rule set. Evaluating a change applies one fixed revision to one submitted change. Authorizing a deployment checks whether an earlier evaluation is still valid at the moment of deployment. Recording what each integration has applied compares the outside world with the intended policy. And the audit record explains which policy, input, and decision led to a consequential action. Those are five responsibilities, and they deserve five clear modules, but nothing about them yet demands five deployed services.

A modular monolith handles them well. PostgreSQL stores policy revisions, evaluations, and authorizations in one transactional domain, and a small worker sends notifications through an outbox. Slack shows status, and Jenkins calls the enforcement API at the moment it deploys. Neither of them decides which policy is in force, which removes a common source of configuration drift before decomposition is even on the table.

Ownership starts to matter when a team proposes a separate integration service. That service can reasonably own delivery attempts, connector credentials, and the revisions each connector reports, but it must never be able to rewrite policy history. The contract between the two carries published revision IDs and event identities, and the policy module has the final say on policy contents. Chapter 12 shows how that contract copes with retries, replay, and integration outages.

Extraction justifies its cost when a capability needs its own deployment cycle, its own resource allocation, or a security boundary the monolith cannot provide. Even then, the extraction needs a single writer for each authoritative record and a verified handoff, because two implementations that can both update the same policy record recreate the dual-write problem. This reasoning fits human resources (HR) platforms, billing systems, support automation, and developer tools. Decide who makes each decision and where its outcome is recorded, and let the deployment topology come from that.

Authorization and Contract Ownership

Separating Catalog, Order, Payment, and Merchant Administration also changes how permissions are enforced. Let’s consider a merchant employee who can read orders and request a refund. Order Service may know which orders belong to a merchant, while Payment Service owns refund state. We have to establish which service verifies the employee’s permission and which one records the result.

A request such as POST /v1/orders/4471/refunds identifies an order, although it does not establish the caller’s access to that order. The gateway authenticates the employee. Order Service may verify that the order exists and belongs to an authorized merchant. Payment Service must verify the refund-specific rules against authoritative payment and permission data before creating a refund operation. An Order Service event saying that a refund was requested cannot be interpreted as proof that it was authorized or completed.

The service contract needs enough information to distinguish a request from a fact. RefundRequested describes an action someone wants performed. RefundCompleted reports the result after the owning service has recorded it. Both require a producer identity and an agreed schema. Neither gives the consumer permission to perform some unrelated action merely because the event arrived on a trusted broker.

Tenant Isolation at the Data Boundary

A SaaS system can authenticate every request correctly and still return another customer’s data. Imagine the employee changes the order ID in the URL from 4471 to 4472. If the service loads the record by ID and only checks that the employee has a merchant role, the request may succeed against another merchant’s order. The resource relationship has to participate in the authorization decision.

One practical approach is to derive the employee’s merchant membership from trusted server-side data and apply that merchant constraint in the query. Listing Listing illustrates a lookup after a service has established the merchant ID from the authenticated principal.

SELECT id, merchant_id, payment_status
FROM orders
WHERE id = $1 AND merchant_id = $2;

This query prevents an order ID alone from selecting a row belonging to another merchant. Authorization is broader than the query, however. The employee may be permitted to read an order and still lack permission to refund it. The application must validate the action, payment state, and refund limits before committing a change. PostgreSQL row-level security can add another enforcement boundary, provided the database roles and tenant context are configured and tested correctly.3

Splitting a service creates a security boundary only if each side enforces it. Two services using the same database credentials can still read or change each other’s tables. Distinct workload identities, scoped database roles, and separate deployment permissions reduce that risk. If Order Service only needs to request a refund, it should not receive direct write access to Payment Service’s refund records.

Authorization Across Asynchronous Boundaries

The ownership decision continues after a request becomes asynchronous. Suppose Order Service records a refund request and a worker dispatches it several minutes later. The worker is authenticated as a service, but its service permission to process queued refunds is separate from the employee’s approval for this particular refund. Chapter 4 described how to bind that approval to an operation and determine whether it must be rechecked before execution.

When authorization depends on data from another service, the owning service needs a documented method to retrieve or verify it. A cached membership list may be sufficient for displaying the refund button, but a privileged financial operation may require a fresher check. If the authorization dependency is unavailable, the system must preserve the pending operation for review or later evaluation rather than treat missing permission evidence as an approval.

Extraction is where these checks tend to go missing. A team extracting the refund workflow into a new service must migrate the resource ownership checks alongside its API and data, and test requests from an employee of another merchant. A successful response to the ordinary checkout path says little about whether the new boundary prevents unauthorized writes.

Summary

The migration outage took a day to fix. The ownership argument after it took a quarter, and that difference is the lesson. Services are boundaries between teams as much as between processes, and a boundary that lets two teams change the same records will go on producing arguments, outages, and release meetings until someone decides who owns what.

The way the teams reached that decision is a good model. They started from the decisions each record supported rather than from the tables, which revealed that one word, product, named two different things. They replaced direct table access gradually, through a local adapter, a contract, a shadow comparison, and finally revoked permissions, so every step could be checked and reversed. They maintained one authoritative writer at every moment of the data transfer. And they treated a modular monolith as a serious option, because a boundary enforced inside one codebase delivers much of the benefit without a network in between.

Once Catalog owned its writes, it could publish changes for others to use. Those events can arrive late, twice, or out of order, and Chapter 12 is about building consumers that cope with all three.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Separate application deployments allow Catalog and Checkout to change independently while both access the product table.
Condition that tests it & A Catalog schema change or failure interrupts checkout, or a shared table or release forces the teams to coordinate.
Constraint or invariant & Catalog controls product writes and consumer contracts, Checkout owns accepted order details, Inventory owns reservation transactions, and database permissions enforce those responsibilities.
Evidence and uncertainty & Verification confirms that direct table access is removed, consumer responses are defined, legacy writers are fenced, and every accepted source change reaches the destination.

Still unknown: how often required synchronous Catalog assessments will interrupt new orders during a Catalog failure, and which operations projections can cover within their freshness contracts.
Signal and evaluation window & Affected operations, shared resource use, and independent rollback results, measured during isolation and migration rehearsals.
Control and decision & Transfer write authority only after source writers are stopped, active transactions are resolved, final changes are applied, and verification passes. Judge the extraction by the release and failure dependencies it was meant to remove.
Owner and review trigger & Catalog owns its migrations and recovery, consumer teams own their integrations and unavailable responses, and product owners resolve eligibility and freshness requirements that affect order acceptance. Review after any change that requires coordinated releases, and before the next extraction.
